reasoning:
The finding holds on both counts. One detail is off: there is no `T(v)` form that emits a check. A non-constant construction goes through `T.checked(v)` (the two compares lowered in MIR), through `T.clamped(v)` (the inline fmin/fmax), or needs no check because of a known range fact. With that correction the substance stands.

1) The spec does not let @fastmath relax range construction. [TYP-9] relaxes "no assumption that values are finite" within the function, but [RNG-3a] says clamped is total and "NaN clamps to the lower endpoint", with no exception. [RNG-6] says NaN is in no range. [RNG-9] makes an out-of-range value undefined behaviour that needs `unsafe`. [PHIL-10] is decisive: a Safe program cannot perform "an invalid range-type construction ([RNG-9])" and "This holds in every build profile and under every manifest setting; no configuration disables a check that this invariant relies on." @fastmath is not `unsafe`. ODR-090 did see the NaN problem inside @fastmath ("the function may be compiled as if no value were NaN"), but it only switched off float facts. It said nothing to make checked or clamped exempt.

2) The NaN can really get through. Neither form is kept apart from the relaxed flags. range_clamp returns an inline expression written straight into the function body. That body sits in `<module>.fastmath.c`, compiled with -ffast-math (clang, gcc) or /fp:fast (MSVC). The diff has no special handling for range construction in the relaxed unit.
- The clamp: under -ffinite-math-only, gcc folds fmax/fmin to MAX_EXPR/MIN_EXPR, whose NaN result is undefined. x86 maxsd/minsd return the second operand when either is NaN, and the operand order is free once NaN is assumed away, so a NaN can come out. Clang marks the maxnum/minnum calls nnan, and under nnan a NaN operand makes the result poison.
- checked: `in_range = (v >= lo) & (v <= hi)`, then a branch on `in_range == 0`. Under finite-math, gcc may invert `!(v >= lo)` into `v < lo`, turning the error test into `v < lo || v > hi`. A NaN is false for both, so it lands in `Ok`. Clang's nnan compares give poison for a NaN operand.
So a NaN range value can leave the @fastmath function and reach strict callers, which trust [RNG-9]/[RNG-6]. Whether a given compiler actually miscompiles a given program is not guaranteed. The flags allow it, and that is enough to break a MUST rule.

correct_fix:
Make [RNG-3]/[RNG-3a] construction strict in every float mode, and make the fix general: one place in the backend for all construction sites, not one per test.
- Emit the float range test and the float clamp as out-of-line runtime helpers, one per representation (f16/f32/f64): something like `ember_rt_range_in_f64(v, lo, hi, inclusive)` and `ember_rt_clamp_f64(v, lo, hi)`. Define them in a unit compiled strict (the runtime or the main unit, never `static inline` in a header the relaxed unit includes).
- Have the relaxed unit call them for every float `checked` and `clamped`. The strict unit can keep the inline forms, since they are correct there.
- Because the relaxed objects are built without /GL or LTO (ADR-085), the call cannot be inlined back into the fast-math code.
- Do not use an inline `isnan` guard instead: -ffinite-math-only folds it to false. A bit-pattern test is possible but fragile under clang's nnan poison, so the strict out-of-line helper is the sound choice.
- Integer range construction is unaffected (no float mode changes integer arithmetic) and stays inline.
- Spec: add to [TYP-9] (or [RNG-3]/[RNG-3a]) that a range-type construction (`checked`, `clamped`) keeps strict IEEE meaning inside `@fastmath`, as [PHIL-10] requires.
- Record the defect in the four documents (ledger, handoff, ADR-085 addendum, spec), and add a test: a `@fastmath` function that clamps and checks a NaN, with a strict caller seeing `lo` and `Err`, run under clang, gcc and MSVC.

reasoning:
The finding holds, though one of its arguments is weaker than it reads. The stronger parts do not depend on that argument.

1. Where the code goes (confirmed). Builtin::FloatLib writes `(isnan(x) != 0)`, `isfinite` and `isinf` straight into the calling function's C. range_clamp writes `fmin(fmax(v, lo), hi)` inline, and its caller at lib.rs:6213 puts that in the calling body too. So inside a @fastmath function all of it lands in `<module>.fastmath.c`. compile_relaxed_object builds that unit with `-fno-fast-math` swapped for `-ffast-math` on clang and gcc, and `/fp:fast` on MSVC. The emitted unit only adds `#pragma GCC diagnostic ignored` for unused functions and variables. Nothing guards NaN. ember_rt.h is included in every unit, so its static inline `ember_ftoi_*` (`if (v != v) return 0;`) is also built with fast-math whenever the relaxed body casts a float with `as`.

2. The weak argument: is `x.is_nan()` a "call" that keeps strict mode? This is contestable. It is declared in std (std/src/math/mod.em:49, a method of `Float` with no body), so a literal reading of [TYP-9]'s "calls keep each function's own" makes it strict. Three things point the other way:
   - [TYP-9] lets @fastmath relax "no assumption that values are finite" within the function.
   - ODR-090 says the function "may be compiled as if no value were NaN".
   - [DET-2] already makes any @fastmath relaxation Nondet, so different answers on different toolchains are not forbidden in themselves.
   The integer methods have an explicit "fixed contracts independent of the caller's lexical overflow policy" sentence in [STD-2] (ODR-084). Float methods have no such sentence. Taken alone, the is_nan folding is arguably a permitted relaxation, or at most a spec gap for an ODR. It is not a clear violation.

3. The [CG-C-2] part holds. [CG-C-2] literally says an accepted program "never produces C that the C compiler rejects or warns about". [TST-27] compiles every accepted test program with warnings as errors on each host compiler. CI runs ubuntu-latest (.github/workflows/ci.yml:21-23), where clang is 18. There, glibc's math.h expands `isnan` to `__builtin_isnan`, and clang 18's default-on -Wnan-infinity-disabled warns on it under -ffinite-math-only. I did not run a compiler (read-only task), so the exact diagnostic is taken from clang 18's known behaviour, not from a local run. On Windows, UCRT's isnan is a call to `_dclass`, so MSVC and clang-on-Windows neither fold it nor warn. That fits the claim that answers differ by toolchain.

4. Clamping is a real violation whatever `is_nan` is. [RNG-3a] says `clamped` is "total ... NaN clamps to the lower endpoint". [RNG-6] says "NaN is in no range". [RNG-9] says producing a value outside its range "is undefined behaviour and needs unsafe", and [RNG-10] lists clamped as a safe way to make a range value. Under -ffinite-math-only, gcc and clang may lower fmax/fmin to maxsd/minsd with any operand order, and those instructions pass NaN through. So Safe code in a @fastmath function can produce a NaN `Roughness` with no `unsafe`. That value leaves the function. For example, `Option[Roughness]` uses NaN as its None value (the empty-slot "niche", [RNG-7]; codegen lib.rs:6936, `ember_f32_is_nan`), so strict code elsewhere would read that `Some(r)` as None. That breaks the owner's rule that the attribute must not change code outside its function. The same exposure plausibly applies to `T.checked`'s comparisons in a relaxed body, and to `as`-to-integer: [TYP-6] says NaN becomes 0, but with `v != v` folded, the NaN reaches `(TYPE)v`, which is undefined in C.

The runtime already has the right tool. ember_rt.h:100-119 tests NaN by its bits, with the comment "so a compiler's floating-point comparison mode cannot hide Option's NaN niche". The new relaxed unit did not apply the same care to the other NaN-defined built-ins.

correct_fix:
Fix it once, for every mode. The spec defines exact results for NaN and infinity in several built-ins: is_nan, is_finite, is_infinite, `T.clamped`, `T.checked`'s range test, and float-to-integer `as`. Emit all of them in a form that no floating-point flag can fold, instead of emitting C float comparisons or <math.h> classification macros:
- Extend the existing bit-test helpers in ember_rt.h (ember_f32_is_nan / ember_f64_is_nan) with is_finite and is_infinite versions.
- Have Builtin::FloatLib's predicates call those helpers.
- Write range_clamp as an explicit NaN bit-test that returns `lo`, followed by the two compares or fmin/fmax.
- Test NaN by its bits in `checked`'s range test (a NaN input fails the check).
- Replace `v != v` in EMBER_FLOAT_TO_INT with the bit test.

Bit tests use only integer operations, so they give the same answer in the strict, contract and fastmath units, and they cause no -Wnan-infinity-disabled warning. That satisfies [CG-C-2], [RNG-3a], [RNG-9] and [TYP-6] without changing the relaxation of real arithmetic inside the function. The alternative, an out-of-line strict helper in the main unit, costs a call per use and is worse.

If the owner wants `is_nan` itself to be relaxable inside @fastmath, that is an ODR question, not something the backend should decide. Even then, clamped and checked must not produce a NaN range value in Safe code, and the C must not warn.

Add a C-gate test: a @fastmath function that uses is_nan, is_finite, `T.clamped(NaN)`, `T.checked(NaN)` and `NaN as i32`, compiled with warnings as errors on clang 18+ (Linux), gcc and MSVC, and run to check the answers are true, false, lo, Err and 0 on every toolchain. Break-test it by reverting to `isnan`.

reasoning:
The facts in the finding are correct, but the violation it claims does not follow from the spec.

Facts that hold: relaxed_gnu_flags only swaps -ffp-contract=off for -ffp-contract=fast (and -fno-fast-math for -ffast-math under @fastmath). relaxed_msvc_flags adds /fp:contract (or /fp:fast). Neither the strict nor the relaxed flag set has -mfma, -march or /arch:AVX2. So on baseline x86-64 the contract object comes out as mulsd + addsd, and the test does pass -mfma itself.

Why this is not a spec violation:
1. What @fp(contract) means is permission, not a guarantee. [TYP-9] says @fp(contract) "permits contraction only". [TYP-9b] says it "permits, and requires the backend to enable" FMA. That reads as the mirror of [TYP-9a], where the implementation "MUST turn it off in the host C compiler". So 9a means contraction off in the host C compiler, and 9b means contraction on in the host C compiler for that function's unit. [CG-C-11] says how: the function goes in "a separate translation unit compiled with the relaxed flags". The code does exactly that. The spec's guaranteed single rounding is a separate feature. [STD-3] says math.fma is single-rounding "on every target; it is how fused arithmetic is written without @fp(contract)". So the spec itself treats @fp(contract) as a permission mode and fma() as the guarantee.
2. The spec never picks a target ISA. The only mention of target-CPU flags is [BEN-5], which only says both sides of a benchmark must match. [CG-C-11] lists the required strict flags (-ffp-contract=off -fno-fast-math, /fp:precise, SSE2 rather than x87 on 32-bit, no flush-to-zero) and names no -mfma or /arch. Whether FMA exists is a property of the target (the CLI's --target), not something the float attribute controls. The perf table line "give one" is not about the instruction set either: it lists fma(a,b,c) next to @fp(contract), and fma() on baseline x86-64 is a libm call, not one instruction. The sentence contrasts roundings, not an ISA promise.
3. Baseline x86-64 is not a toolchain that "cannot honour" the attribute. E9041 is for a toolchain that cannot relax floating point for one function. gcc, clang and MSVC all can, and the code tells them to. The contraction is allowed and the compiler would use FMA if the target had it. On AArch64, where FMA is baseline, the same flags do fuse. Nothing is silently dropped ([PHIL-12]/[TYP-9c]): the function builds under the relaxed mode.
4. The fix the finding implies would break the spec's spirit. Adding -mfma or /arch:AVX2 to relaxed units only would mix ISA levels inside one program. The relaxed object would crash with an illegal-instruction fault on CPUs without FMA/AVX2. -mfma also allows AVX encodings across the whole unit, which changes code beyond the multiply-add. That trades a permissive optimisation for a portability failure, and a float attribute would be changing the program's target requirements. Emitting E9041 on every baseline x86-64 build would also be wrong, because the attribute is honoured there.
5. The -mfma in a_relaxed_unit_is_compiled_to_fuse copies the existing D-325 test (the_c_compiler_never_fuses_a_multiply_and_an_add). It checks that the flags allow fusion where the target has the instruction, which is the only thing the flags control.

Possible follow-up, not a defect: if the owner wants contract code to fuse on x86-64, that is a target/CPU-level setting (for example a manifest or --target feature applied to every unit alike). It is outside [TYP-9b] and would need an owner ruling. The ADR could also say plainly that on baseline x86-64 @fp(contract) permits fusion but produces none unless the target enables FMA.

reasoning:
The finding is wrong because the prelude's min, max and clamp involve no float operation that @fastmath can change.

1. How they are lowered. min, max and clamp are expanded in the calling body through pick_less / pick_greater, which becomes `b if TotalLess(b, a) else a`. The C backend emits TotalLess on a float as a call to the runtime function ember_total_lt_f64 / ember_total_lt_f32 (or _f16). That function compares the two values' bit patterns as integers (total_key_f64(a) < total_key_f64(b)). The runtime is compiled strict and lives outside the fastmath translation unit. Even if it were inlined there, it is integer work, and no float mode changes integer work; ODR-090 rests on that same point for integer facts. So the result is always exactly one of the operands, bit for bit. There is no float arithmetic and no IEEE comparison in the fastmath unit that finite-math or NaN-free assumptions could fold. Whatever both operands are known to satisfy, the result satisfies too.

2. The operand facts are already gated. picked_ranges is filled only from range_of(a) and range_of(b). The facts that @fastmath makes unsound are the ones from float arithmetic and from comparison arms, and both are gated:
- float Unary and Binary go through float_facts_hold (lines 23179 and 23201);
- comparison-arm facts check `self.active_fp != FpMode::Fast` (line 22281).
What reaches min/max ungated is only a literal's own value, a range type's declared bounds, or a local's recorded fact. The Block arm only takes the hull of those.

3. What the rule means. The rule's own reason is "as the function may be compiled as if no value were NaN", and ODR-090 explains it as "a comparison's arm then proves nothing". Both point at facts whose truth depends on an operation the relaxed unit may compile differently. Read word for word, "no fact about a float is derived" would also forbid the literal arm (Int/Float, line 23168) and the range-type arm (line 23163). Those are just as ungated as the min/max arm, the finding does not flag them, and dropping them would buy no soundness. ODR-090's options are about how far the fact ban reaches: option 2, the one ruled, bans float facts and keeps integer facts. Nothing in the ruling targets selection by totalOrder.

So no fact the Block arm produces inside @fastmath can be false, and it matches both the rule's reason and the ruling's intent. The spec wording could say "derived from a float operation or comparison" to match, but that is a wording note, not a compiler defect.

reasoning:
The finding mostly holds. One part is wrong: top-level extern fn declarations are already rejected.

1. What the spec's table says. The @fastmath / @fp(contract) row applies to "fn" only. The Part X row just above it applies to "fn, interface method". The table names "interface method" as its own position, so "fn" does not cover one. [ATT-1] says an attribute on a declaration it does not apply to is E0104. So @fastmath on an interface method must be E0104. The compiler instead checks every interface member with site "fn" (lib.rs:26975, 26993), so the attribute passes.

2. Could an interface method's @fastmath pass to implementations? No. [TYP-9] makes the mode lexical: "instantiation, inlining and calls keep each function's own." No spec text passes a float mode from an interface or abstract declaration to the method that implements it. The code agrees: method_signature takes fp only from the method's own attributes (lib.rs:7491), and a bodyless interface member is skipped when methods are registered (lib.rs:7573).

3. Is accepting it and doing nothing a violation? Yes. An abstract class method is a "fn", so its site check passes, and its Signature gets an fp mode (lib.rs:7565-7577, 7491). But it has no body, and codegen drops abstract and extern-declaration bodies from the relaxed units (codegen_c lib.rs:130 filters `!body.is_abstract && !body.is_extern_declaration`). So the attribute is accepted and has no effect. That is what [ATT-6] forbids ("never accepts and ignores it"), and [TYP-9c] says "The attribute is never ignored ([PHIL-12])." A bodyless interface method has the same outcome, and also breaks [ATT-1].

4. Where the finding is wrong. A top-level `extern fn` declaration (is_foreign_decl) goes through the foreign-declaration branch, which checks every non-@ffi/@safety attribute with site "extern item" (lib.rs:26938). The same happens inside an extern block (in_extern gives "extern item", lib.rs:26944). The fastmath row lists only "fn", so both already give E0104. A sibling hole the finding missed: extern class members (ItemKind::ExternClass, lib.rs:26977) are also checked with member site "fn", so they have the same accept-and-ignore problem.

Net: the violation is real for bodyless interface methods (breaks [ATT-1], [ATT-6] and [TYP-9c]), abstract class methods ([ATT-6], [TYP-9c]) and extern class members. It is not real for extern fn declarations.

correct_fix: Choose the attribute check's member site by what the member is, not only by MemberKind::Fn, so the fix covers every bodyless-method case at once. In check_item_attributes (compiler/ember_typeck/src/lib.rs around 26991), give interface members the site "interface method". Also add "interface method" to the Part X attribute row (noalloc/nosync/…/deterministic/realtime), because the spec lists them there. Then @fastmath/@fp on any interface method becomes E0104 ("applies to: fn") under [ATT-1]. For a class member with no body (an abstract virtual method) and for extern class members, @fastmath/@fp should also be E0104 with a note that a float mode governs a body and each implementation or override carries its own ([TYP-9]: "calls keep each function's own"). The simplest general way is to treat a member with `decl.body.is_none()` as a declaration site, not "fn", for body-scoped attributes (fastmath, fp, and likewise overflow). Do not pass the mode on to implementing methods: the spec makes the mode lexical per function. Add reject conformance tests under tests/conformance/TYP-9/ (or ATT-1): @fastmath on a bodyless interface method, and @fp(contract) on an abstract class method.

reasoning:
The line the finding quotes is not in the current working tree. `grep "in_mode = fp != self.active_fp"` and `grep same_in_every_float_mode` both find nothing in compiler/. The code that exists at that spot (compiler/ember_typeck/src/lib.rs:34891-34927) deals with `mut` defaults directly. When the callee's float mode differs from the caller's and the checked default does float work, a `Mode::Mut` default sets `not_in_mode = true`. That produces E0900 ("the default of `{name}` does float work in its function's `{mode}` mode, which a call from here cannot keep yet"), and the default becomes an ExprKind::Error. It is not evaluated in the caller's mode. `git diff HEAD` has this `if mode == Mode::Mut {` branch as an added line, so the uncommitted work already includes the fix and the finding was reviewing an older draft.

On the finding's sub-questions: yes, a `mut` default is a place, and a place can contain float work, for example an index `a[(x * 2.0) as usize]`. `float_work` (lib.rs:35548) catches that case. `Index` recurses into its index, and `Cast` returns true when its source or target is a float. Kinds it does not list fall to `_ => true`, so it errs on the side of reporting. A mut place with float work is therefore rejected with a diagnostic, never miscompiled. It cannot become a closure, because a closure cannot return a writable place. That is the only honest outcome short of a larger redesign, and it matches ADR-085's promise: "If a closure cannot hold a default ... E0900 says so; the default is never evaluated in the wrong mode". A place with no float work (a name, a field, an integer index) means the same in every mode, so using it in place is correct.

One small point, not this finding: ADR-085 cites `[TYP-9c]` for the E0900. In the spec, `[TYP-9c]` is about E9041, a toolchain that cannot honour the attribute. The citation is loose, but that is a documentation nit, not the silent wrong-mode evaluation this finding alleges.
